name: Sturgeon's Law
statement: Ninety percent of everything is crap.
meaning: In any field, the vast majority of what is produced is mediocre — and that is normal, not a sign the field is worthless.
mechanism: Quality is hard and rare; most output clusters near the average, with only a thin top slice of excellence. Judging a whole field by its bulk is therefore misleading, because the bulk of anything — books, music, science, startups — is unremarkable almost by definition. The exceptional is, always, the exception.
example: A critic dismisses science fiction by pointing at its worst pulp. Sturgeon's reply: of course most of it is dross — so is most of every genre; judge the field by its best.
whyItMatters: It is a defence against cherry-picking: you cannot damn a whole category by its worst examples, because ninety percent of every category is weak. It reframes evaluation around the top of the distribution rather than the mass.
misreadings: The '90%' is rhetorical, not a measurement, and 'crap' means mediocre, not evil. It is not cynicism or a claim that nothing is good — it is the opposite, a case for judging things by their finest work rather than their most abundant.
origin: Coined by the science-fiction author Theodore Sturgeon around 1957–58 — he called it 'Sturgeon's Revelation' — while defending the genre against critics who cited its worst work. His original word was 'crud', not 'crap'.

sources.text: Sturgeon, T. (March 1958). Book column, Venture Science Fiction ('Sturgeon's Revelation').
